source_excerpt: 以玉作六器，以禮天地四方：以蒼璧禮天，以黃琮禮地，以青圭禮東方，以赤璋禮南方，以白琥禮西方，以玄璜禮北方。皆有牲幣，各放其器之色。
source_excerpt_translation_worker_gloss: With jade are made the six vessels, to serve Heaven, Earth and the four directions: with the blue-green bi disc serve Heaven, with the yellow cong tube serve Earth, with the green gui tablet serve the East, with the red zhang serve the South, with the white hu serve the West, with the black huang serve the North. All with victims and silks, each according to its vessel's colour. (worker gloss; no published translation inspected this session)

passage_support.excerpt: chinaknowledge: 'It was compiled during the Warring States period 戰國 (5th cent.-221 BCE)…'; 'Zheng Xuan believed in the authenticity of the Zhouli as a book compiled on the order of the Duke of Zhou…, while many others considered it to be a forgery or a text concocted at a much later date.'; 'After all it must be concluded that only a few parts of the text were compiled during the Han, and not, as many scholar had argued, the whole book.' passage_support.supports: The 'later prescriptive text' half of entry line 116 at reference-work level: majority scholarly dating places the transmitted Zhouli in the Warring States (about the 3rd century BC, i.e. later than the Neolithic/Shang specimens the entry warns about), with a documented Han-era editorial history and a live forgery controversy (Zhu Xi's Liu Xin attribution; Qing critics Wan Sitong/Yao Jiheng/Fang Bao; Kang Youwei) that the retrieved sources themselves record.
passage_support.does_not_support: No single agreed date: Western-Zhou-date holdouts persist, and Wang Zhong/Wang Guowei argued only parts (e.g. ritual-music sections) are Warring States. None of these sources dates the bi/cong clause individually; chinaknowledge is a scholarly reference work (cites Boltz 1993, Liu Qiyu 1992, Nylan 2001) and Wikipedia is tertiary.

passage_support.locator: WHE: section 'Liangzhu Culture Jade', paragraphs 1-2; Łakomska: section 'Jade animal figurines', discussion of the Fanshan cong (article pp. 14, incl. footnote 25); UH Press: Asian Perspectives 53(2) article listing, Lopes abstract; Rawson sample: Introduction, p. xxii (running footer 'Copyrighted Material XXii')
passage_support.excerpt: WHE: 'This theory is challenged, however, because there is no documentation from the Liangzhu Culture linking the objects directly to the concepts of earth and heaven. The earth-heaven motif is understood to have developed later during the Shang Dynasty, and those who challenge a cosmological interpretation of the cong and bi point out that one cannot interpret Neolithic artwork from the later perspective of the Shang.' Łakomska: 'Congs may have been used in Earth's thanksgiving rituals. The form of the earth was then perceived as rectangular and the sky as round.' and 'As suggested by David Keightley, the congs, for example, could have been used as a "stalk container for offering plants", or, as Deng Shuping suggests, plinths, or joints for wooden posts.' Rawson: 'The abundant transmitted writings, generally taken as the foundation of early history, were not usually from the same time as the events they described. They were compiled, sometimes centuries later, handed down and edited over hundreds of years.'
passage_support.supports: The entry's methodological caution at line 116 that the bi=Heaven / cong=Earth formulas need a dated textual argument before being made the original meaning of Neolithic or Shang specimens. A retrieved scholarly article presents competing cong-function hypotheses (ritual/cosmological vs plant-stalk container vs plinth/post-joint), and the retrieved reference-work passage states there is no Liangzhu documentation for the Heaven/Earth link and warns against reading Neolithic art from the later Shang perspective. Rawson (the entry's own R95 author) independently supports the general transmission principle.
passage_support.does_not_support: None of these passages identifies what any specific Neolithic or Shang specimen meant; they document a debate and a caution, not a positive identification. The Lopes abstract (checked this round) frames the iconography debate generally and does not itself state the cong/bi reinterpretation argument (see negative sweep S4). WHE is a tertiary encyclopedia (it cites Childs-Johnson for the cosmological side).

passage_support.excerpt: 欽定周官義疏 凡例: '一周官有古文今文異本賈疏云劉向未校之前㦯在山巖石室有古文考校後為今文鄭據今文注故云故書作某盖故書即古文也其杜子春鄭司農所讀有異同者竝列焉' ; '一漢武帝求遺書得周官五篇司空職亾漢人以考工記附之名曰冬官非其實也兹稱考工記以従其朔'. 總目提要: '《周禮》一書不盡原文，而非出依託，可概睹矣。' and, listing contradictions between the Zhouli and other classics, '而《儀禮•聘禮》…與《掌客》之文不同。又《大射禮》…與《司射》之文不同。《禮記•雜記》載子、男執圭與《典瑞》之文不同。《禮器》…與《司幾筵》之文不同。' and '《考工記》稱鄭之刀，又稱秦無廬，鄭封於宣王時，秦封於孝王時，其非周公之舊典，已無疑義。' and '大抵《周官》六典，其源確出周公，而流傳既久，不免有所竄亂'.
passage_support.supports: The entry's demand that the formula carry 'a dated textual argument' before use: the transmitted text has a documented editorial history — the 1748 imperial edition lists 故書/古文 versus 今文 variant readings (Du Zichun, Zheng Zhong) and rules that the Han substitution of the 考工記 for the lost 冬官 '非其實' (is not the fact); the Siku editors state the text is 'not wholly original but is not a fabrication' and list concrete disagreements between Zhouli clauses and other classics (聘禮/掌客, 大射禮/司射, 雜記/典瑞, 禮器/司幾筵). The same apparatus dates the 考工記 to pre-Qin by internal evidence (鄭之刀/秦無廬) — a worked example of exactly the dated textual argument the entry asks for.
passage_support.does_not_support: This is an 18th-century imperial apparatus with its own commitments ('其源確出周公'), not a modern critical edition: no 十三經注疏 collation, no 孫詒讓《周禮正義》 and no manuscript/slip evidence was inspected. The variant list concerns the text's internal consistency and transmission, not the bi/cong clause's date or meaning.
